lessons.title: FSI 1 · Morning greetings
theory: Two men greet each other in the morning. Jambo works at any hour; Habari za asubuhi? asks specifically for the morning's news, and Njema answers that all is well.
Mutisya: “Jambo, bwana.” — Hello, sir.
Sangai: “Jambo.” — Hello.
Mutisya: “Habari za asubuhi?” — How are you this morning?
Sangai: “Njema.” — Fine.

Source: Foreign Service Institute (U.S.), Swahili Basic Course, 1963. — Public domain (U.S. Government work). The dialogue is reproduced from the public-domain course transcript; summaries and quiz questions are original Bolingo writing.

questions.explain: In the dialogue, “Habari za asubuhi?” is answered by “Njema.” — Fine.
“Habari za asubuhi?” means “How are you this morning”.

lessons.title: FSI 2 · Daytime greetings
theory: The daytime greeting swaps Jambo for Hujambo? — literally “do you have no trouble?” — and answers Sijambo, “I have no trouble.” Habari za mchana? asks after the day's news.
Sangai: “Hujambo, bwana.” — Hello, sir.
Mutisya: “Sijambo.” — I am fine.
Sangai: “Habari za mchana?” — How are you today?
Mutisya: “Njema.” — Fine.

Source: Foreign Service Institute (U.S.), Swahili Basic Course, 1963. — Public domain (U.S. Government work). The dialogue is reproduced from the public-domain course transcript; summaries and quiz questions are original Bolingo writing.

lessons.title: FSI 3 · Evening greetings
theory: Evening greetings follow the same pattern with Habari za jioni? (How is the evening?) or Habari za usiku? (How is the night?). Habari njema answers “the news is good”.
Sangai: “Jambo, bwana.” — Hello, sir.
Mirambo: “Jambo, bwana.” — Hello, sir.
Sangai: “Habari za jioni?” — How are you this evening?
Mirambo: “Habari njema.” — The news is good.

Source: Foreign Service Institute (U.S.), Swahili Basic Course, 1963. — Public domain (U.S. Government work). The dialogue is reproduced from the public-domain course transcript; summaries and quiz questions are original Bolingo writing.

lessons.title: FSI 4 · Greeting a lady
theory: A man greets an older woman as mama (ma'am, mother), and she answers Sijambo. The morning question and answer stay the same, so only the address changes.
Hamisi: “Hujambo, mama.” — Hello, ma'am.
Mrs. Kirambo: “Sijambo.” — I am fine.
Hamisi: “Habari za asubuhi?” — How are you this morning?
Mrs. Kirambo: “Njema.” — Fine.

lessons.title: FSI 8 · Breakfast at the hotel
theory: At a hotel breakfast, the waiter asks Je, unataka chakula? (Would you like food?). Kuna chakula gani? asks what is available, and Tafadhali, niletee mayai orders eggs politely.
Waiter: “Je, unataka chakula?” — Would you like some food?
Aramian: “Ndiyo, bwana.” — Yes, sir.
Aramian: “Kuna chakula gani?” — What food is there?
Waiter: “Kuna matunda na uji na mayai.” — There is fruit, porridge, and eggs.
Aramian: “Tafadhali, niletee mayai.” — Please bring me eggs.

Source: Foreign Service Institute (U.S.), Swahili Basic Course, 1963. — Public domain (U.S. Government work). The dialogue is reproduced from the public-domain course transcript; summaries and quiz questions are original Bolingo writing.
